newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgaria investment to shrink if reform fails.
newsitem.headline: Bulgaria investment to shrink if reform fails.

text.p: Foreign investment in Bulgaria will shrink further if the government fails to speed up market reforms which have been delayed over the past seven years, foreign investors say.
"We have no prospects for further investment in Bulgaria until the uncertainty is sorted out," Raiffeisenbank Bulgaria general manager Douglas Dryden told Reuters.
"Bulgaria is the only country for which we have worked out a scenario which includes serious reduction of our activity."
Failure to carry out market reforms by Bulgaria's eight revolving-door governments since the collapse of communism in 1989 has turned the country into the "sick man of Europe".

"Bulgaria is one of the few places where there is danger of total financial collapse while the world economy is growing," Richard Ran, an economist and president of U.S. sports equipment importer Novecon, told journalists.
Slow and reluctant privatisation, lack of investment incentives and inconsistently applied legislation have deterred foreign investors.
Foreign investments total less than $1 billion in a country seen as the least favourable business environment in the region, foreign businessmen say.
Cumulative inflation for first 11 months of this year topped 224 percent and the central bank's main interest rate is 180 percent. The lev fell from 70 in January to 500 on Monday.
"Short-term planning in this situation is one day and medium term is one month," Nestle Sofia General Manager Dimitris Koronakis told Reuters.
The Bulgarian subsidiary of Swiss foods producer Nestle SA sees sales next year declining by 50 percent due to the country's grave crisis.

Other foreign companies in Bulgaria also expect their businesses to shrink. They say there is still chance for the economy to recover and they are still prepared to wait for the government to step up reform, but if nothing happens they would consider pulling out at the end of next year.

A car-making joint venture between Rover Group Ltd, a subsidiary of German automotive group Bayerische Motoren Werke AG (BMW) and a Bulgarian consortium, closed down in April complaining of lack of government support.
Bulgaria is debating the introduction of a tough currency board regime to restore confidence in the financial system.
Some $800 million in personal savings have been withdrawn from the ailing banking system in the past half year, central bank figures show.

Under the currency board system, the central bank will not be able to print levs it cannot cover with hard currency reserves, which is expected to remove political pressure from monetary policy. The bank will also be banned from lending to the government and commercial banks.

"The understanding that the currency board in and of itself will save Bulgaria is illusionary. There is an entire package of structural and economic reforms that must be implemented on a simultaneous basis," Ran said.

"I think that some people are under the illusion that the IMF will unblock the money for the currency board and all will be well. That is not true," said Ran, who met with senior government officials and bankers in Sofia last week.

Failure to meet reform targets including closing or restructuring loss-making state enterprises has practically suspended funding from the World Bank, and the International Monetary Fund has twice postponed a $115 million credit until the government fulfils a July agreement to close 64 lossmakers and ban credits for 70 problem firms.
The IMF may ask Bulgaria to complete the reform programme agreed in July before disbursing further support for the implementation of the currency board plan, said Ran.

Bulgaria will have access to its maximum annual limit of more than $700 million in IMF loans granted only in extraordinary circumstances and the government was given to understand that it may qualify when it introduces the currency board, bankers said recently.
